scenarios.title: Rosewood Manor: The Case Opens
scenarios.context: Rosewood Manor stood dark against the storm on the night Alden Rosewood died. Alden, sixty-eight, was the manor's owner — a self-made and famously ruthless collector of art, debts, and secrets, who had called the household to dinner to announce changes to his will. At five past eight a sound of breaking glass came from the study; when the door was forced, Alden lay dead beside his overturned desk, and the room had been locked from the inside. Before weighing a single clue, the detective asks you, the assistant, to meet the people beneath this roof. Mina Rosewood, his niece and ward, whose allowance Alden had threatened to cut off only that week. Dev Ashcombe, his business partner, ruined by a deal Alden blamed on him. Iris Vale, his quiet private secretary, who kept the house's every secret — including one Alden held over her. Ronan Rosewood, his estranged son, struck from the will years ago and returned uninvited. And Pia Rosewood, his much-younger wife, whom he had lately spoken of divorcing. Below stairs wait the witnesses: Mrs. Vale, the longtime housekeeper and Iris's mother; Tom, the gardener; and Adeline, the live-in nurse. Five suspects, one locked room, and a single night to set in order. Begin, as any careful mind must, by gathering the facts.
scenarios.prompt: Before any code is written, what should the assistant collect first so the investigation can proceed in proper order?
objectives: Treat the case as a sequence of clues
Prepare to work step by logical step

# Gather the known people and places
def gather_facts():  # Collect suspects and rooms
    suspects = [  # List of five suspects
        "Mina", "Dev", "Iris", "Ronan", "Pia"  # Names
    ]  # Close suspect list
    rooms = ["study", "library", "hall"]  # Key rooms
    return {"suspects": suspects, "rooms": rooms}  # Facts

# Inspect the initial case details
case_board = gather_facts()  # Build starting facts
count = len(case_board["suspects"])  # Count suspects
print("Suspect count:", count)  # Output total

subSteps.title: Meet the household
body: The detective sets five photographs on the hall table, face up. "Mina. Dev. Iris. Ronan. Pia," she says, tapping each one. "Everyone in this house wanted something from Alden Rosewood. Before tonight ends, one of them will have taken everything."

subSteps.title: Order before deduction
body: "A careless mind leaps at the answer," the detective says. "A careful one lays out what it knows." In your notebook, that means keeping facts in named collections rather than loose thoughts — a list you can point at, count, and cross off.
Nothing here is judged yet. Tonight we only gather.

subSteps.title: The board is set
body: Five names now hang on the evidence board, and beneath them, the shape of the night: a locked study, broken glass, a dinner called to rewrite a will.
You have not accused anyone yet — and that is precisely the point. A case solved in proper order begins with facts laid end to end. The witnesses are waiting to be heard.

scenarios.title: Rosewood Manor: The First Statements
scenarios.context: With the household known to you, the detective lays three witness notes on the table — a word from Mrs. Vale the housekeeper, another from Tom the gardener, and a third from Adeline, the nurse who sat with Alden each evening. None can be trusted until it is set in order, for the notes are messy: full of nicknames, stray punctuation, and uneven spacing. Nothing is judged, the detective reminds you, until it is placed in proper form.
scenarios.prompt: How would you turn the messy witness strings into clean records before you compare the clues?
objectives: Store each clue in a structured record
scenarios.sampleReasoning: I would split each line into speaker, time, and clue so the statements are easy to compare later.
scenarios.idealSolution:
# Cut each note at the speaker mark
def parse_statement(note):  # Clean one statement line
    clean = note.replace(" - ", ": ", 1)  # Fix dash mark
    speaker, _, quote = clean.partition(":")  # Split at colon
    clue = quote.strip().strip("'\"")  # Strip outer quotes
    res = {"speaker": speaker.strip()}  # Speaker record
    res["clue"] = clue  # Add clue field
    return res  # Return clean record

# Test the cleaner on witness notes
witness_notes = [  # List of raw witness statements
    "Mrs. Vale: 'Glass broke at 8:05 pm.'",  # Note 1
    "Tom - 'Blue coat at rose arch at 8:10.'",  # Note 2
]  # Close statement list
for note in witness_notes:  # Step through every note
    print(parse_statement(note))  # Print structured record

witnessStatements: Mrs. Vale: 'Glass broke by the study at 8:05 pm.'
Tom: 'A blue coat passed the rose arch at 8:10 pm.'
Nurse Adeline says:   'The hall clock read 8:12 when the lights flickered.'
Mrs. Vale admits: 'I saw Iris enter at 8:02, but hid it.'

subSteps.title: Three notes, three hands
body: Mrs. Vale writes in a housekeeper's neat hand but signs herself formally. Tom spells phonetically and separates his words with dashes. Nurse Adeline pads her lines with nervous spaces. Three accounts — and not one writes like the others.
Spread side by side, the notes refuse to line up. The detective slides them toward you. "Clean these. I don't care how they arrived. I care what they say."

subSteps.title: Every statement has a seam
body: Look closely at any note: there is always a natural seam where the speaker ends and the clue begins — usually a colon, sometimes a dash. Find the seam once, and every note can be opened the same way.

In Python, partition() cuts a string at its first seam and hands back the pieces; strip() trims the ragged edges left over. That is all "parsing" means here: find the seam, split, tidy. No magic — just careful scissors work.

subSteps.title: The notes agree at last
body: Cleaned and aligned, the three statements finally sit level on the desk: glass at five past eight, a blue coat by the rose arch at ten past, lights faltering at twelve past.

One suspect has moved into view already — someone was near the rose arch between those sounds. But times written by three different hands cannot yet be trusted to order. The clock itself must be interrogated next.

scenarios.title: Rosewood Manor: Sorting the Timeline
scenarios.context: The three statements now read plainly, yet each carries a time in its own careless format — one written with a colon, one with a full stop, one bare of any mark at all. The detective taps the hall clock and observes that time itself does not lie; only the records of it do. Until every moment is written the same way and set in sequence, the true order of that evening — Mrs. Vale's breaking glass, the blue coat by the rose arch, Adeline's flickering lights — stays hidden.
scenarios.prompt: How would you normalize those times and sort the events from earliest to latest?
objectives: Convert each value to the same comparable format
scenarios.sampleReasoning: I would turn every time into one standard datetime value first, then sort the events by time.
scenarios.idealSolution:
# Import the clock parser tool
from datetime import datetime  # Tool to parse time text

# Normalize and sort the times
def sort_timeline(times):  # Order events chronologically
    def to_clock(text):  # Standardize single time string
        clean = text.replace(".", ":")  # Change dot to colon
        clean = clean.upper().replace(" ", "")  # Strip space
        return datetime.strptime(clean, "%I:%M%p")  # Datetime
    return sorted(times, key=to_clock)  # Sort by clock order

# Replay the evening in sequence
study_clock = ["8:12 pm", "8:05 pm", "8.10 PM"]  # Statements
print(sort_timeline(study_clock))  # Display sorted times

subSteps.title: The clock is questioned
body: The detective carries the cleaned statements to the grandfather clock in the hall and reads each time aloud: "eight oh-five p m... eight point one zero capital P M... eight colon twelve pm." She lets the inconsistency hang in the air.
"Time did not write these," she says. "People did. And people are careless. We will teach their words to agree — then, and only then, may the evening be replayed in order."

subSteps.title: Comparable before sortable
body: Here is the trap: "8:05 pm" and "8.10 PM" are both perfectly readable to a person, but to a machine they are just different shapes of ink. You cannot sort what you cannot compare.

So the work happens in two moves. First, normalize — scrub every variation into one agreed form (a real datetime value). Second, sort — which becomes trivial once every item speaks the same language. Notice how sorting was never the hard part; agreement was.

subSteps.title: Replay the seven minutes
body: Set in sequence, the night compresses into seven telling minutes: the glass breaks at 8:05, the blue coat crosses the rose arch at 8:10, the hall lights shudder at 8:12.
Whoever broke the glass had five minutes alone near that wing before anyone stirred. The detective circles the interval twice. "This gap is where our answer lives."

subSteps.title: Make the times tell the truth
Five minutes of shadow
body: The timeline now stands in the detective's hand like a confession waiting for a name. Glass at 8:05. Blue coat at 8:10. Flickering lights at 8:12.

You have converted chaos into sequence — and sequence has already bought you something: a five-minute window in the west wing that no innocent explanation has yet claimed. Next, the alibis. Gaps in them will do what none of the confident voices will: speak.

scenarios.title: Rosewood Manor: Alibi Gaps
scenarios.context: One by one the detective questions the five who had reason to wish Alden gone. Mina speaks of the conservatory and the kitchen; Dev swears he never left the library; Iris allows that she crossed the front hall and looked into the study; Ronan insists he stayed among the instruments in the music room; and Pia says she lingered in the gallery until the alarm. Set against the rooms a witness could actually vouch for, it is the gaps — the rooms no one saw them in — that speak louder than any suspect's confident tone.
scenarios.prompt: How can you compare the suspect claims against the witnessed rooms to find contradictions?
objectives: Spot which claim cannot be true
scenarios.sampleReasoning: I would compare the claimed rooms with the witnessed rooms and flag any room that appears in one set but not the other.
scenarios.idealSolution:
# Find claims without witness support
def unverified_rooms(seen, claimed):  # Locate alibi gaps
    unseen = set(claimed) - set(seen)  # Subtract seen rooms
    return sorted(unseen)  # Return missing rooms in order

# Compare the manor room lists
witnessed = ["study", "front hall", "library"]  # Seen rooms
claimed = [  # All rooms claimed by suspects
    "conservatory", "kitchen", "library",  # First set
    "front hall", "study", "gallery"  # Second set
]  # Close claimed list
print(unverified_rooms(witnessed, claimed))  # Print gaps

suspectClaims.claim: I was in the conservatory and kitchen after 8:00.
I stayed in the library the whole time.
I checked the front hall, then the study.
I never left the music room.
I was in the gallery until the alarm rang.

subSteps.title: Five voices, five certainties
body: One at a time they give their accounts, and not one of them hesitates. Mina among her plants. Dev behind library doors. Iris brisk in the front hall. Ronan with the instruments. Pia drifting through the gallery.
The detective writes nothing down while they speak. Afterwards she says: "Notice how certain they all were. Certainty is cheap. What matters is which of those rooms anyone else could swear to."

subSteps.title: What overlaps tells the truth
body: Claims come in lists; truth lives in the comparison. Put every claimed room in one pile and every witnessed room in another — then stop reading the piles and start reading the space between them.

A set difference answers one question cleanly: which claimed rooms appear in no witness account at all? Those rooms are where alibis go to die. Two piles, one subtraction, and the confident tones stop mattering.

subSteps.title: Two theories eliminated
body: The subtraction is merciless. The conservatory, kitchen, music room, and gallery — every one of them claimed, none of them witnessed. Four alibis now rest on rooms where no witness can place a soul.

But look at the other edge of the blade: only Iris willingly places herself near the study — the room where Alden died. Two comfortable theories have just been eliminated, and three suspects remain standing. The manor is getting smaller.

scenarios.title: Rosewood Manor: The Constraint Solver
scenarios.context: Now the detective spreads the whole affair out as a grid: the five suspects — Mina, Dev, Iris, Ronan, and Pia — set against five rooms, five possible weapons, and five recorded times, with a short list of clues that any true answer must satisfy. There is nothing for it but patience: try one arrangement, test it against every clue, and the instant a single fact refuses to fit, set that theory aside without drama and try the next.
scenarios.prompt: How would you write a recursive solve() function that tries one assignment at a time and backtracks when a clue fails?
objectives: Try one option at a time
Undo bad choices when a path fails
scenarios.sampleReasoning: I would choose one suspect-room-weapon-time combination, check every clue, and backtrack as soon as a choice breaks a rule.
scenarios.idealSolution:
# Check if room fits the clues
def fits_clues(suspect, room):  # Check known clue rules
    if room == "study" and suspect == "Ronan":  # Rule check
        return False  # Ronan was seen outside study
    return True  # Room is consistent with clues

# Try rooms and backtrack on breaks
def solve(suspects, rooms, plan):  # Recursive assignment
    if not suspects:  # When every suspect has a room
        return plan  # Return consistent assignment
    suspect = suspects[0]  # Take the next suspect
    for room in rooms:  # Test each remaining room
        if fits_clues(suspect, room):  # If clues allow
            plan[suspect] = room  # Tentatively place suspect
            rem = rooms - {room}  # Remaining room options
            res = solve(suspects[1:], rem, plan)  # Recurse
            if res:  # If valid path found
                return res  # Return solved arrangement
            plan.pop(suspect)  # Backtrack failed placement
    return None  # No valid combination found

# Run the solver for the suspects
suspect_list = ["Mina", "Dev", "Iris"]  # Suspect list
room_pool = {"study", "library", "hall"}  # Open rooms
print(solve(suspect_list, room_pool, {}))  # Output match

subSteps.title: Too many theories for one mind
body: The detective rules a grid across half the desk: five suspects down the side, and across the top — five rooms, five weapons, five recorded times. Five names crossed with fifteen possibilities. She does not bother counting the arrangements aloud; the number is absurd, and it is meant to be.
"No one solves a mansion in one leap," she says. "We solve it the way it was made: one decision at a time. Start with a single suspect. Give them a room. See if the night survives that much."

subSteps.title: One choice at a time
body: Here is the whole trick, and it fits in a sentence: solve the case for one suspect, then hand the smaller case — same rules, one fewer suspect, one fewer room — to another detective exactly like yourself.

That hand-off is what a recursive call is. Each call makes one placement and delegates the rest; when the final call receives an empty list of suspects, there is nothing left to decide, and it reports success. You never wrote a plan for five suspects. You wrote a plan for one, plus the courage to delegate.
subSteps.snippet:
def solve(assignments, suspects, rooms):
    if not suspects:              # nobody left to place: done
        return assignments
    suspect = suspects[0]
    for room in rooms:            # try ONE placement...
        result = solve(assignments + [{"suspect": suspect, "room": room}],
                       suspects[1:], rooms - {room})   # ...then delegate
        if result:
            return result
    return None

subSteps.title: When to abandon a theory
body: Now suppose the very first placement — Mina in the study — already puts the rope in the study. Clue three says the rope never entered that room. Does it matter that four more placements might have worked out beautifully? No. The theory is dead at its first fact.

Abandoning a branch the instant it contradicts a clue is called pruning, and it is the entire reason this method finishes before dawn. Check early, fail fast, erase quietly — assignments.pop() is the sound of a theory being withdrawn without drama. What remains after every dead branch is pruned can only be the truth.
subSteps.snippet:
if not respects_clues(candidate, assignments):
    continue          # prune: this theory died at its first broken clue
assignments.append(candidate)
result = solve(...)
if result: return result
assignments.pop()     # unwind the failed theory, try the next room

subSteps.title: One arrangement still stands
body: Branch by branch, the grid collapsed: every arrangement that put the rope in the study withered at clue three; every theory that left the library figure in a blue coat died at clue four. Hundreds of theories were born and buried in the time it took to pour the tea.

Exactly one arrangement survived every clue at once — and it points, unfashionably, at the quietest person in the house. The detective reaches for the drawing-room bell. It is time to gather everyone and say it aloud.

scenarios.title: Rosewood Manor: Case Solved
scenarios.context: The storm has passed, and the household is gathered once more in the drawing room — Mina and Ronan, Dev and Pia, and Iris quietest of all. Calmly, and in order, the detective retraces the single thread that held: the breaking glass at five past eight, the study locked from within, the figure in the blue coat by the rose arch, and the one alibi that could not survive them all. Every wrong turn had been discarded along the way, and what remained could only be the truth.
scenarios.prompt: In one or two sentences, what clue proved the case and how did the step-by-step search keep the answer honest?
objectives: Connect the clue to the final solution
Reflect on the value of orderly reasoning
scenarios.sampleReasoning: The case turned on the blue coat witness and the study timing. The recursive search worked because it rejected any assignment that broke a clue and kept only the path that fit all of them.

# Format the decisive case finding
def summarize_case(clue, guilty):  # Case conclusion summary
    return f"Guilty: {guilty}. Key clue: {clue}"  # Summary

# Output the final case deduction
proof = "blue coat at 8:10 pm"  # Decisive clue sighting
print(summarize_case(proof, "Iris Vale"))  # Final reveal
scenarios.reveal: The corrected clock puts Iris Vale in the study at 8:05. She used the service door and a hidden curtain thread to pull the locked door shut after leaving. Tom's blue coat sighting at 8:10, Mrs. Vale's protective lie, the missing corrected will, and Alden's threat all point to Iris. The room looked impossible only because its clock and exit were misread.

subSteps.title: The drawing room gathers
body: Rain still ticks against the windows as the household assembles — Mina pale, Dev composed, Ronan insolent, Pia restless, and Iris with her hands folded, watching the carpet.
The detective stands with her back to the cold fireplace and begins, unhurried, at five past eight.

subSteps.title: Skills you used to crack this case
body: Only now, with the case closed, does it deserve saying: you did not merely follow a story — you worked like a programmer.

Parsing turned messy testimony into clean records. Normalizing and sorting datetimes rebuilt the true order of the night. Set differences exposed the alibi gaps. Recursion with pruning searched an impossible grid and kept only what survived every clue. Each one was discovered in service of the case — which is exactly how the best knowledge is kept.
